title: Advent: The Christmas Story
intro: The Christmas story through the days of Advent, from the prophets' promises to the night in Bethlehem.

posts.display: If only You would rend the heavens and come down, so that mountains would quake at Your presence.
posts.caption: Advent, from the Latin adventus, "coming," is the season of the four Sundays before Christmas. Today is the first, when many churches light the first candle of an Advent wreath, often for hope. This verse is from a lament late in Isaiah, prayed by God's people with Jerusalem and its temple in ruins: they beg God to tear open the sky and come down. Advent begins with that longing. Starting today, 27 days through the Christmas story.

In the 730s BC, King Ahaz of Judah was terrified of an attack by two neighboring kings. The prophet Isaiah offers him a sign of reassurance: a child called Immanuel, Hebrew for "God with us," and before the boy can tell right from wrong, the threat will be gone. The Hebrew almah means a young woman; the ancient Greek has "virgin." Jewish readers often see the sign fulfilled in Isaiah's day, while Christians read it as pointing to Jesus.

The northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, around Galilee, had been overrun by the Assyrian empire, and 2 Kings 15 records their people being taken captive. Isaiah promises that the region that suffered first would see a great light: rescue and new life after disaster. Centuries later, Matthew's Gospel quotes this passage when Jesus begins his work in Galilee.

After picturing the oppressor's rod broken and the boots of battle burned, Isaiah announces the birth of a royal child, who will rule from David's throne with justice and lasting peace. His grand titles describe that ideal king, and "Prince of Peace" became one of the best-known Christian names for Jesus. Jewish tradition has often read the child as King Hezekiah, Ahaz's son. Handel set this verse to music in his oratorio Messiah, first performed in 1742.

Isaiah 11 pictures David's royal family tree cut down to a stump, with a new shoot growing from the roots of Jesse, David's father. This verse describes the king that shoot will become: filled with God's spirit, wise and fair, judging the poor with justice rather than by appearances. Ancient Greek and Latin versions read "piety" here and keep "fear" in the next verse, giving the traditional "seven gifts of the Holy Spirit." The shoot also inspired the Advent Jesse tree.

About a century after Isaiah, the prophet Jeremiah watched Judah's last kings fail as Babylon closed in. He repeats the promise with a similar image: a "righteous Branch" for David, a king who would finally rule with justice. The prophet Zechariah later uses "the Branch" almost as a name for this hoped-for king.

Micah, who prophesied around the same time as Isaiah, names a small town: Bethlehem, a few miles south of Jerusalem and the hometown of King David. Ephrathah was an old name for the clan and area around it. A new ruler for Israel would come from the same humble place David did. Matthew's Gospel later quotes this verse.

The second Sunday of Advent, when many churches light a second candle, often for peace. Isaiah 40 opens with "Comfort, comfort My people," words to Jewish exiles in Babylon, and promises a road home through the desert with God leading the way. All four Gospels apply this verse to John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Jesus.

Malachi spoke to Judah after the return from exile, when people were asking, "Where is the God of justice?" This is God's answer: a messenger will come first to prepare the way, and then the Lord himself will come to his temple. Malachi later names that messenger as the prophet Elijah, and many Jewish families still set out a cup for Elijah at the Passover meal. In most Christian Bibles, this is the last book of the Old Testament, leading straight into the Gospels.

Luke's Gospel opens in the temple in Jerusalem. An elderly priest named Zechariah has been chosen by lot to burn incense, a rare honor, when an angel appears beside the altar. He and his wife Elizabeth had grown old without children, and the news is that his prayer has been heard: they will have a son, who will prepare the people for the Lord. His name, John, comes from the Hebrew Yochanan, "the LORD has been gracious."

The angel Gabriel is sent to Nazareth, a small village in Galilee, to Mary, a virgin engaged to Joseph, a descendant of King David. His greeting ("Hail, full of grace" in the old Latin) troubles her, so he reassures her, then gives the news: she will have a son and name him Jesus. Commentators note the contrast with Zechariah's vision in the temple: this announcement comes to an unknown young woman in an out-of-the-way village.

Gabriel tells Mary she will have a son named Jesus, and describes him in royal terms. About a thousand years earlier, according to 2 Samuel 7, God promised King David that his throne would last forever. By Mary's time, no descendant of David had been king for nearly 600 years, so Gabriel's words revive that old promise.

Mary had asked how this could happen, since she was a virgin. Gabriel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her, adding that "no word from God will ever fail." Her reply is simple trust: she accepts God's plan, even though an unexplained pregnancy could bring her shame. It's often called her fiat, from the Latin for "let it be." The scene is known as the Annunciation, a favorite subject of painters for centuries.

Mary hurries to the hill country of Judah to visit her relative Elizabeth, now in her sixth month. When Mary arrives, Elizabeth's unborn son, the future John the Baptist, leaps, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, honors Mary as "the mother of my Lord." Commentators see Luke's point: even before birth, John is already pointing to Jesus. With Gabriel's greeting, Elizabeth's words form the first part of the Hail Mary. This meeting is known as the Visitation.

The third Sunday of Advent is traditionally called Gaudete Sunday, from the Latin for "rejoice," and in many churches today's candle is rose-colored, for joy. Fittingly, this is Mary's answer to Elizabeth's blessing: a song of joy that gives all the credit to God. It's called the Magnificat, the first word of its Latin version, and for centuries it has been sung daily at evening prayer in many churches.

Mary's song turns the usual order of the world upside down: rulers fall, the humble are lifted up, the hungry are fed. It closely echoes the song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2, sung by another woman after God gave her a son. In Greek, Mary's verbs are in the past tense, as if God's great reversal has already happened.

Elizabeth, childless into old age, gives birth to the son the angel promised, and her neighbors see it as Luke does: a sign of God's great mercy. On the eighth day, at his circumcision, relatives expect him to be named after his father. Elizabeth says no, and Zechariah, unable to speak since the angel's visit, writes on a tablet, "His name is John." At once his voice returns.

With his voice restored, Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, sings. His song celebrates that God has come to rescue his people, keeping promises made to David and Abraham, and says his own newborn son will prepare the way. It's called the Benedictus, from its first Latin word, "Blessed," and is sung at morning prayer in many churches. It ends by picturing the Messiah as sunrise: "the Dawn will visit us from on high."

Matthew tells the story from Joseph's side, and tells readers at the outset that Mary's child is from the Holy Spirit. A betrothal then was a binding agreement, and ending it required a formal divorce. Finding Mary pregnant, Joseph, "a righteous man," plans to end it quietly rather than shame her in public. From today until December 23, many churches sing the "O Antiphons," the centuries-old prayers behind "O Come, O Come, Emmanuel."

Joseph has decided to end his engagement quietly, but before he can act, an angel speaks to him in a dream. The message changes his plan: he should not be afraid to take Mary as his wife, because her child is God's doing. "Son of David" points back to the royal family tree that opens the chapter. Joseph is guided by dreams several times in Matthew, like his namesake in Genesis, the famous dreamer; Matthew even gives both men a father named Jacob.

The angel tells Joseph what to name the child. Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yeshua (Joshua), which means "the LORD saves," so the angel's explanation plays on the name itself. It was a common name at the time. Many scholars note that by naming the child, Joseph takes him as his own legal son.

The fourth Sunday of Advent, when the last of the four candles on many Advent wreaths is lit, often for love. Matthew quotes Isaiah's sign to King Ahaz from earlier in this plan, and translates Immanuel for his readers. The idea frames his whole Gospel, which ends with Jesus saying, "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20).

Luke sets the story on a world stage. An inscription from the time of Augustus, the first Roman emperor, hails his birthday as the beginning of "good news" for the world. Many readers see a deliberate contrast: the emperor's decree sets events in motion, but Luke's real good news is a child born in a small town. Scholars still debate the census itself, since the best-known one, under Quirinius, came around 6 AD.

Joseph travels from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the small town Micah had named centuries earlier, because he belongs to David's family line. Bethlehem means "house of bread" in Hebrew. The journey would have taken several days on foot. Luke never mentions a donkey; that familiar detail comes from later tradition.

Mary, engaged to Joseph and expecting her child, makes the journey with him, so the birth takes place in Bethlehem, David's own town. Luke says only that the time came "while they were there." He doesn't describe a frantic search on the night they arrived, as many Christmas plays do, and they may have been in Bethlehem for some time. Christmas is now two days away.

Christmas Eve, and the story reaches the birth itself. Luke tells it in one plain sentence, and the point is in its humble details: the promised king's first bed is a manger, a feeding trough for animals. Newborns were commonly wrapped snugly in strips of cloth. The Greek word translated "inn," kataluma, can also mean a guest room, so many scholars picture a crowded family home with animals kept close by.

Merry Christmas. In the fields near Bethlehem, where young David once kept his father's sheep, shepherds are keeping watch by night when an angel appears. The news comes first to ordinary working people, and it is "for all the people": the Savior has been born, the Christ, or Messiah, the anointed king the prophets promised. That's the Christmas story. Thank you for walking through Advent with me.
